column4: In the raised houses, God's name is remembered and He is glorified morning and evening; this supplies the worship setting whose practitioners are described in 24:37.
Trade does not distract these men from ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ or إِقَامِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةِ; with 24:36, remembrance, glorification, prayer, and the purification term zakat form the section's single practice.
The command joins reciting the Book to establishing prayer, then names prayer's restraining work and ذِكْرُ ٱللَّهِ; it directly fuses recitation, prayer, moral effect, and remembrance.
God commands Moses, وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكْرِى, making prayer an enacted form and purpose of remembrance.
The believers are commanded to remember God abundantly; 33:42 adds glorification and 33:43 answers with God's own salat upon them.
وَسَبِّحُوهُ بُكْرَةً وَأَصِيلًا turns abundant remembrance in 33:41 into repeated glorification at set parts of the day.

هُوَ ٱلَّذِى يُصَلِّى عَلَيْكُمْ gives the other direction of the salat root: after human remembrance and glorification in 33:41-42, God and His angels turn toward the believers and bring them from darkness to light.
وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ commands remembrance of the Lord's name morning and evening; 76:26 continues the same practice bodily.
Night worship is staged as prostration followed by prolonged glorification, فَٱسْجُدْ لَهُ وَسَبِّحْهُ, completing the named remembrance of 76:25 with bodily prayer.
فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَكُن مِّنَ ٱلسَّٰجِدِينَ directly places glorification and prostration in one commanded act.
Those reminded by God's signs fall prostrate and glorify their Lord's praise; reminder, bodily prayer, and tasbih become one response.
Every creature is said to know صَلَاتَهُ وَتَسْبِيحَهُ, an explicit pairing that supports the section's treatment of prayer and glorification as one practice.
At the call to Friday prayer, believers are told فَٱسْعَوْا۟ إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ; the congregational prayer itself is approached as remembrance.
After the Friday prayer, abundant remembrance continues into ordinary movement and is tied to success, linking the section's remembrance-prayer sequence to فلاح.
Satan's aim is to obstruct both عَن ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ وَعَنِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةِ; the paired obstruction confirms that remembrance and prayer belong to one practice.
When prayer is completed, remembrance continues standing, sitting, and lying down; the verse binds salat, dhikr, and bodily positions before prayer is re-established in safety.
وَلَا تَجْهَرْ بِصَلَاتِكَ وَلَا تُخَافِتْ بِهَا sets an audible middle course for prayer, directly realizing the section's dictionary sense of جهر in prayer and recitation.
Zechariah is قَآئِمٌۭ يُصَلِّى فِى ٱلْمِحْرَابِ when the angels call; this embodies prayer as standing and follows his supplication in 3:38.
Zechariah is commanded to remember his Lord much and glorify at evening and morning, extending the prayer and supplication scene of 3:38-39 into dhikr and tasbih.

The command joins charity that purifies and increases purity, تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِم, with the Prophet's prayer over its givers, وَصَلِّ عَلَيْهِمْ; it closely parallels the section's purification-salat link.
God and the angels perform salat upon the Prophet, then believers are commanded to perform salat upon him; one ayah displays the root's divine and human directions together.
وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا ٱلْقُرْءَانَ لِلذِّكْرِ explicitly joins the Qur'an's being made easy with remembrance, bringing together the section's recitation, ease, and dhikr.
The repeated formula that the Qur'an is made easy for remembrance makes recurrent practice, rather than a one-time hearing, part of the connection.
This third occurrence again identifies facilitated Qur'an engagement with dhikr, matching the section's inclusion of reading within remembrance.
The fourth refrain completes the surah-long insistence that the Qur'an has been made easy for remembrance.
فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ joins ease, the reciter's tongue, and remembrance, precisely developing the section's account of dhikr circulating on the tongue.
The surah opens with ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ and closes in 96:19 with prostration and nearness; its command-to-bodied-worship arc closely parallels this section's opening and completion.
The forbidden act is stopping عَبْدًا إِذَا صَلَّىٰ, placing a servant's actual prayer between the opening command to recite in the Lord's name and the closing command to prostrate.
وَٱسْجُدْ وَٱقْتَرِب closes the surah by turning the opening recitation in the Lord's name into the servant's bodily worship.
The command to establish prayer names قُرْءَانَ ٱلْفَجْرِ within its daily span, making Qur'an recitation an expressly prayer-shaped act.
Those who recite God's Book and establish prayer are named in one sequence; the verse directly joins the section's reading and salat.
An upright community recites God's signs during the night وَهُمْ يَسْجُدُونَ, joining voiced recitation with the bodily movement of prayer.
When the revelation is recited, the knowledgeable fall on their chins in prostration; 17:108 supplies their spoken glorification.
Their response within the recitation-prostration scene is سُبْحَٰنَ رَبِّنَا, so the tongue's tasbih accompanies the body's fall described in 17:107.
They again fall on their chins, now weeping and increasing in humility; the ayah completes the bodily effect of recitation and spoken glorification in 17:107-108.
When the Merciful's signs are recited, the prophets fall سُجَّدًا وَبُكِيًّا; hearing revelation immediately becomes embodied worship.
وَٱذْكُرِ ٱسْمَ رَبِّكَ وَتَبَتَّلْ إِلَيْهِ directly echoes remembering the Lord's name and presents it as undivided devotion.
فَٱقْرَءُوا۟ مَا تَيَسَّرَ مِنَ ٱلْقُرْءَانِ and وَأَقِيمُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ put feasible recitation and established prayer in the same concluding instruction.
لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِۦ لِسَانَكَ addresses the physical tongue during reception of the Qur'an; 75:17-18 identify God's collecting and reciting followed by the Prophet's recitation.
God assumes responsibility for gathering the revelation and قُرْءَانَهُ, paralleling the promise that the Prophet will be made to recite without losing it.
When God has recited it, the Prophet is told فَٱتَّبِعْ قُرْءَانَهُ; divine imparting becomes the reciter's voiced following.
The command joins inward, humble remembrance with speech below full loudness, دُونَ ٱلْجَهْرِ مِنَ ٱلْقَوْلِ, and ends وَلَا تَكُن مِّنَ ٱلْغَٰفِلِينَ, opposing heedless worship.
The angels neither disdain worship nor tire: they glorify God and prostrate to Him, completing 7:205's quiet remembrance with tasbih and bodily submission.
فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ is the closest formulaic parallel to the section's opening command, substituting the epithet “the Magnificent” for “the Most High.”
The same command, فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ, returns near the surah's close, showing repeated glorification of the Lord's name as a framing act.
The surah closes with فَسَبِّحْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلْعَظِيمِ, an exact structural analogue for worship organized around glorifying the Lord's name.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord's praise before sunrise and sunset and at portions of night and day, giving the practice a prayer-like daily rhythm.
The command to glorify with the Lord's praise before sunrise and sunset establishes the daily rhythm continued through night and prostration in 50:40.
Night glorification and أَدْبَٰرَ ٱلسُّجُودِ explicitly place tasbih beside the embodied act of prostration.
فَسُبْحَٰنَ ٱللَّهِ حِينَ تُمْسُونَ وَحِينَ تُصْبِحُونَ orders glorification across evening and morning; 30:18 completes the daytime cycle with praise.
وَلَهُ ٱلْحَمْدُ ... وَعَشِيًّا وَحِينَ تُظْهِرُونَ adds praise and the remaining daily times to 30:17's glorification.
Believers are commanded to bow, prostrate, worship, and do good لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ; bodily prayer is directly tied to the success named beside prayer in the section.
God's house is purified for circumambulation, retreat, bowing, and prostration; a purified place gathers the bodily acts that the section's prayer definition enumerates.
The purified House is assigned to those circling, standing, bowing, and prostrating, staging worship through its named places and movements.
The prayer under danger is enacted by standing with the Prophet, taking arms, prostrating, and yielding place to another group; salat is visibly a coordinated sequence of bodily acts.
The faithful are worshippers and praisers as well as ٱلرَّٰكِعُونَ ٱلسَّٰجِدُونَ, combining verbal devotion with prayer's bowing and prostration.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّىٰهَا reproduces the section's success-through-purification claim and helps explain why divine salat and human prayer are linked through تزكية.
قَدْ أَفْلَحَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ states success, and 23:2 immediately identifies their humble prayer as its first concrete mark.
The successful believers are فِى صَلَاتِهِمْ خَٰشِعُونَ; prayer is the enacted disposition following the success announced in 23:1.
In the embodied pressure of battle, believers are commanded to remember God abundantly لَّعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ, directly linking dhikr with success.
The warning to “those who pray” makes the prayer label alone insufficient; 107:5 identifies heedlessness toward their own prayer as the fault.
عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ سَاهُونَ reverses the section's recitation without forgetting: a bodily prayer emptied by heedlessness is condemned.
Hypocrites rise lazily to prayer, display themselves, and remember God only a little; their standing reproduces prayer's body while severing it from sincere dhikr.
When the Qur'an is recited to them, they do not prostrate; the refusal reverses the recitation-to-prostration response in 17:107 and 19:58.
The congregation leaves the Prophet standing when trade or amusement appears, enacting the distraction that 62:9 forbids and reversing the undistracted worshippers of 24:37.
Wealth and children must not distract believers from God's remembrance; those distracted are the losers, reversing the section's dhikr-to-success relation.
The hypocrites come to prayer only lazily; outward attendance without willing worship is a concrete boundary around the section's integrated practice.
They are called to prostration but cannot perform it, though they had been called while sound; bodily capacity without prior obedient practice has been lost.
When commanded ٱرْكَعُوا۟ they do not bow, a direct reversal of prayer as obedient bodily movement.
Moses asks for Aaron's aid so that “we may glorify You much”; 20:34 gives the paired purpose of remembering God much.
وَنَذْكُرَكَ كَثِيرًا completes 20:33's abundant glorification and shows the two verbal acts as one shared mission.
Zechariah calls upon his Lord for good offspring; his supplication becomes standing salat in 3:39 and remembrance-tasbih in 3:41, illustrating the dictionary claim that prayer is dua.
أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ عَلَيْهِمْ صَلَوَٰتٌ مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ gives salat a divine subject and human recipients, exemplifying the root's direction from God toward His servants.
The sincere Bedouin treats his spending as nearness to God and as a means to صَلَوَٰتِ ٱلرَّسُولِ, showing salat as supplication offered for another person.
The inhabitants of Paradise begin their supplication with سُبْحَٰنَكَ ٱللَّهُمَّ and end with praise, joining dua, tasbih, and praise as one uttered worship act.
Jonah's cry from darkness includes سُبْحَٰنَكَ inside his supplication, making glorification itself the language of prayer in distress.
“Call upon Me; I will answer you” is followed by calling that act عِبَادَتِى, giving a Qur'anic bridge for the section's dictionary statement that prayer is both dua and worship.
The command to establish prayer is immediately embodied as وَٱرْكَعُوا۟ مَعَ ٱلرَّٰكِعِينَ, displaying bowing as part of communal salat.
Guarding the prayers is followed by وَقُومُوا۟ لِلَّهِ قَٰنِتِينَ, making upright bodily standing an element of sustained prayer.
Under fear prayer may be performed walking or riding; once safe, remembrance resumes, joining bodily adaptation of salat to taught dhikr.
Mary is commanded to be devout, prostrate, and bow with those who bow, gathering distinct prayer movements in one instruction.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night before their Lord سُجَّدًا وَقِيَٰمًا, pairing prostration and standing as one nightly practice.
The devout worshipper passes the night سَاجِدًا وَقَآئِمًا while fearing the Hereafter and hoping for mercy, giving prayer its paired bodily postures and inward stance.
The believers are seen رُكَّعًا سُجَّدًا seeking God's bounty and approval; bowing and prostration visibly mark their worship.
فَٱسْجُدُوا۟ لِلَّهِ وَٱعْبُدُوا۟ closes the surah by converting an imperative into the body's prostration and worship.
وَأَنَّ ٱلْمَسَٰجِدَ لِلَّهِ identifies prostration places as belonging to God and forbids calling upon another there, joining place, bodily worship, and dua.
The summons “when you rise to prayer” introduces washing of face and limbs, and the verse closes with God's desire to purify the believers; bodily preparation and purification surround salat.
Prayer is commanded at the two ends of day and near night, and good deeds remove evil deeds; its repeated daily form is assigned a cleansing moral effect.
The revelation is made easy بِلِسَانِكَ so the Prophet can announce good news and warning; it supports the section's movement from facilitated recitation to words circulating on the tongue.
The “best discourse” makes skins shiver and then soften, together with hearts, إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ; recited revelation becomes remembrance with an embodied effect.
The signs God recites to the Prophet are also called ٱلذِّكْرِ ٱلْحَكِيمِ, directly grounding the section's dictionary sense of Qur'an recitation as dhikr.
The revelation is explicitly ُذِكْرٌۭ وَقُرْءَانٌۭ مُّبِينٌۭ, identifying reminder and Qur'an while excluding poetry.
God calls the sent-down revelation ٱلذِّكْرَ and promises to guard it, supplying the object whose reading the section counts as remembrance.
God says وَأَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ ٱلذِّكْرَ so the Prophet may explain what was sent, identifying the recited revelation itself as dhikr.
The revealed scripture is هَٰذَا ذِكْرٌۭ مُّبَارَكٌ, supporting remembrance as engagement with the Qur'an rather than only an independent formula.
The Qur'an is called ذِكْرٌۭ لَّكَ وَلِقَوْمِكَ, making revelation a remembrance borne by the Prophet and his people.
The unbelievers nearly strike the Prophet down with their looks لَمَّا سَمِعُوا۟ ٱلذِّكْرَ; dhikr here is an audible recitation, and 68:52 identifies its universal scope.
وَمَا هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌۭ لِّلْعَٰلَمِينَ completes 68:51's scene of hearing, showing the recited message itself as remembrance.
When the Qur'an is recited, listeners are commanded to attend and be silent; it supplies the receptive counterpart to voiced reading as worship.
If speech is made public, God knows the secret and what is still more hidden; this closely parallels the section's aloud-hidden boundary around voiced worship.
Whether speech is concealed or made public, God knows what breasts contain; the ayah extends the جهر boundary from audible words to inward intention.
ٱدْعُوا۟ رَبَّكُمْ تَضَرُّعًا وَخُفْيَةً stages dua in humility and privacy, supplying the quiet side of prayer as uttered supplication.
Zechariah calls his Lord نِدَآءً خَفِيًّا, a concrete private-voice counterpart to the section's discussion of prayer or recitation made aloud.
فَٱذْكُرُونِىٓ أَذْكُرْكُمْ joins commanded remembrance to reciprocal divine remembrance and immediately to gratitude, one of the acts included in the section's dictionary definition of dhikr.
وَٱذْكُر رَّبَّكَ إِذَا نَسِيتَ makes remembrance the direct remedy when forgetting occurs, clarifying the section's movement between being made to recite, not forgetting, and remembering.
The Prophet must not obey one whose heart has been made heedless of God's remembrance, marking inward heedlessness as the opposite of sustained dhikr.
Satan makes a people forget ذِكْرَ ٱللَّهِ; this is the explicit reversal of remembrance preserved against forgetting.
After naming God's beautiful names, the ayah says all in the heavens and earth glorifies Him; divine name and universal tasbih meet in one statement.

The surah opens with all creation glorifying God and later turns human listeners toward Friday prayer and remembrance in 62:9-10, echoing the section's structural movement from tasbih to enacted worship.
The Prophet is told to seek forgiveness and glorify his Lord's praise evening and morning, combining verbal worship with a repeated daily rhythm.
The Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord's praise حِينَ تَقُومُ; “when you rise” gives tasbih a bodily setting continued at night in 52:49.
Night and the retreat of the stars extend the glorification commanded in 52:48 across the worshipper's daily cycle.
The closing command joins glorifying the Lord's praise with seeking His forgiveness, exemplifying tasbih as a broad verbal act of worship.
